In addition, on a transcript, majoring in a "Department" rather than a "Program" may also be perceived by employers and graduate programs as more substantial and equal to majors in other "Departments." As a department, with equal recognition and validation as all other departments, socially justice-minded prospective students and young scholars whose work, teaching, and passion are grounded in gender, equal rights, and social justice work will be all the more drawn to courses and majoring or double majoring in GWS. • Enhance the connections between many URI departments and faculty involved in the study of gender, equality, and social justice.
Department designation will encourage more administrators, faculty, and students to affiliate and collaborate with GWS.
Research indicates that where an organization has status differentials, including between a "Department"' and a "Program," cross- pollination and collaboration are less likely to occur.
As the GWS Department, other departments and administrators will be inclined to take GWS more seriously and reach out more to GWS as equal stakeholders.

4 • Bring URI in line with colleges and universities around the country, including universities URI aspires to and competes with for students and faculty.
There are approximately 800 universities around the country that have acquired Department status and others, like us, are seeking it.
In RI, no other college or university currently has department designation for their GWS programs.
As a Flagship University, URI should be at least up to par with our peer or "aspiring-to-be-like" institutions. "Thinking Big," URI should strive to be a leader in education and organizational design.
In RI, especially, URI should be the first to accomplish this important goal. • Attract highly competitive and diverse faculty who wish to be part of a fully recognized "Department" rather than "Program." In promotion and tenure decisions, it is also possible that working for a "Department" will be seen as more valuable, permanent, and reputable than working for a "Program." • Create growing interest in GWS leadership.
As a Department with a "Chair" instead of a "Director," faculty might be more interested in taking on the position as "Chair" of Gender and Women's Studies. • Attract external funding.

As a Department, getting grants for an individual or a department as a whole may have more credibility than getting grants for a "Program." To external funders and reviewers, programs may appear more ad hoc and less permanent than departments.
Those seeking to support research and scholarship are likely to seek more permanent "homes" for resource allocation. • Send a powerful message to all URI alumni and to GWS alumni conveying URI's commitment to the value, teaching, and scholarship of gender and women's studies, including a focus on: LGBTQ rights, black lives matter, the Me Too Movement, and global human rights.
Showing alumni the unequivocal support for a Department of GWS will perhaps catalyze more gift giving, scholarships, and further endowments. • Send a powerful message of support to URI students, faculty, and staff who are women, LGBTQ, nonbinary, and males advocating for equal rights URI's commitment to the value, teaching, and scholarship of gender and women's issues.
C.
INSTITUTIONAL ROLE: The organizational change should be clearly related to the published role and mission of the institution and be compatible with the organizational structure of the institution 1.

Explain how the organizational change is consistent with published role and mission of institution and how it is related to institutional planning.
GWS strongly aligns with URI's 2016-2021 Academic Strategic Plan GWS upholds Goal 1: Enhance Student Success-Strategies 1, 2, 3 GWS, anchored in interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary methodologies, offers URI students a unique educational experience from which they learn not only the complex root causes of all forms of devaluation of human life and nature, but also how to overcome them through human agency.
Our transformative curriculum comes alive through our students, their actions, and their success at URI and beyond.
GWS gives URI students the education and skills to thrive and lead in a multicultural, diverse, antiracist world and workplace.
Foundational to the GWS program is praxis: theory and action.
We transmit to our students the know-how and skills to create the world they want to live in through timely coursework that includes engaged learning opportunities here and abroad.
Through mentorship, GWS faculty encourage students to strive, lead, and transform their lives and those of

5 others for the better.
Experiences with action projects, field assignments, on and off campus activism, and public service shape the character and education of our students.
GWS students are visible, active, and inspiring to each other and other students at URI.
More than 90% of our students are double majors.
They integrate what they learn in GWS courses with their other major(s).
Through our majors, GWS contributes to and fortifies the discourse on human rights, anti-racism, dignity, equality, and social justice throughout the curriculum and across the disciplines.
Strongly aligning with Strategy 3, a critical element of the GWS formula of student success is to provide a dynamic and fluid curriculum that combines the traditional classroom, online courses, faculty-supervised internships, field trips (including to Washington DC), study abroad, and participation in topical programs.
GWS also offers a Graduate Certificate Program that has been operational for many years now, with a total of more than 25 graduates, and a history of graduate studies collaborations with English, History, Psychology, and Political Science.

GWS upholds Goal 2: Expand Research, Scholarship and Creative Work-Strategies 1, 4 GWS sustains interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary research and scholarship through its faculty's research programs, institutional curricular and research collaborations (AAF, LAX, Honors, Nonviolence and Peace Studies, and nearly all A&S departments), academic journals (Dignity and Journal of Feminist Scholarship), and programming (F18 Honors Colloquium on Reimagining Gender, Dana Shugar Colloquium, Feminisms in Action Lectures, Schweer Lecture on Gender and Public Health, the new Gender and Race Lecture, more).
GWS faculty engage in international research (Latin America, Europe, and Asia) and work in areas with policy implications, especially in human and sex trafficking, reproductive rights, sexual violence, and environmental justice.
In line with Strategy 4, our students have exciting opportunities for undergraduate and graduate research.
GWS has a research group in human and sex-trafficking supervised by Dr.
Donna Hughes.
Through their collaboration with Dr.

Hughes, students have been successful in presenting at conferences, publishing research, and securing coveted graduate school offers and professional positions.
GWS upholds Goal 4: Embrace Diversity and Social Justice-Strategy 2 and 3 GWS' mission as a discipline is to center human rights, equality, dignity, anti-racism, and social justice in all we do.
GWS does this especially well through its transformative and topical curriculum by offering courses that include Black Feminisms, Black Masculinities, Latinx Masculinities, Transgender Lives and Cultures, and other courses in the field of Queer Studies.
Central to this mission, is a yearly program of events that prioritizes diversity, inclusion, and social justice.
GWS actively recruits a variety of students and is one of the most diverse discipline on campus.
We have the highest number of students of color and other minoritized groups among our majors and minors.
Through our scholarship funding, GWS prioritizes need-based decisions and the fair distribution of resources across eligible students.
GWS also has a single-mother Carlson scholarship that offers the student full-tuition for the duration of their matriculation.

As a Department, GWS is poised to extend anti-racist principles and actions at URI, the RI community, and beyond.
GWS embodies key URI Strategic Goals, in particular in the area of Embrace Diversity and Social Justice.
The designation of GWS as a Department goes hand in hand with the demand for an Africana Studies Department.
GWS joins African Studies in upholding the core values of diversity, inclusion, antiracism, and social justice in all areas of academic life at URI.

6 We join AAF and other departments in advancing a more diverse, inclusive, and anti-racist university that will better serve our community of students, faculty, administrators, and staff. 2.
Explain how the organizational change impacts other units and programs within the institution.
Have you communicated with the other units and programs and have any concerns been raised relative to the organizational change?
Describe the concerns.
GWS becoming a department does not impact other departments and programs.
As discussed above, GWS has operated as a department for many years without impacting other academic units.
Rather, GWS has collaborated closely with other academic units to uphold its interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary discipline.
With department designation, GWS will fortify and broaden collaboration across the disciplines.
D.
INTERINSTITUTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS: The organizational change should be consistent with all policies of the Council on Postsecondary Education pertaining to the coordination and collaboration between public institutions of higher education. 1.

Estimate the projected impact of the organizational change on the other public higher education institutions in Rhode Island (e.g., loss of students or revenues), provide a specific rationale of the assumptions make in the projections, and indicate the manner in which the other public institutions were consulted in developing the projections.
Have you communicated with other institutions about the organizational change and have any concerns been raised related to role, scope, and mission or duplication?
URI will lead the way in RI by creating a Department of Gender and Women's Studies.
Regionally, there are several departments that include UMass-Dartmouth, Connecticut College, Wellesley College, and Simmons College.
None of our similar peer institutions has departments in Women's Studies (JMU, UNH, UVM, etc.).
Of our "aspire to be like" peer institutions, the University of Delaware and University of Virginia have departments in Women's Studies, UCONN does not.
This moment offers an ideal opportunity for URI to take a leadership position by designating GWS as a department and rise to the level of two out of three "aspiring to be like" institutions.

There will be no impacts to other RI institutions in terms of loss of students or revenue.
Nearly 99% of our majors come from within URI and select GWS as a second major in their sophomore year or as a first semester junior.
All major RI public and private institutions offer Women's Studies or similar programs like Gender and Sexuality Studies.
These institutions have successfully recruited students for their programs over the years.
There is no reason to believe that a change in GWS designation as a department will change that pattern. 2.
List and describe any cooperative arrangements with other institutions relative to the organizational unit. (Signed copies of any agreements pertaining to the use of faculty, library, equipment, and facilities should be attached.)

7 GWS does not have cooperative agreements with neighboring institutions at this time but does aspire to work more consistently to build a stronger network of similar departments and programs locally and regionally.
The goal will be to enhance future research and programmatic collaborations and student learning opportunities. 3.
If external affiliations are required, identify providing agencies (indicate the status of any arrangements made and append letters of agreement, if appropriate.) No external affiliations are required to deliver the GWS curriculum or support other activities.
E.

Describe the facilities and capital equipment (e.g., classrooms, office space, laboratories, and telecommunications equipment) and assess the adequacy of these resources relative to the purpose of the unit and to the requirements of the Americans with Disabilities Act and state disability statutes.
GWS does not require new facilities and capital equipment for this change.

GWS has been housed in Roosevelt Hall since its establishment as a program in 1978.
GWS will remain at its current location on the third floor of Roosevelt Hall and occupy the same offices of 317, 315, 313, 311, 316 and 314.
We have a seminar room, 311, that we use for multiple purposed such as small classes, faculty and student meetings, workshops, candidate interviews, and social events.
GWS courses are scheduled across the university via general scheduling and we use Roosevelt 311 for our smaller classes.
All spaces are in compliance with ADA requirements. 2.

Identify the anticipated expenditures related to the organizational change; include the costs of personnel, operations, equipment, facilities and other resources.
Indicate by source anticipated revenues to support the proposed change.
NOTE: Excel budget forms (Rhode Island Office of Postsecondary Commissioner https://www.riopc.edu/page/academic_program/ ) are self-calculating.
GWS does not require new resources for this structural change.
GWS already functions as a department with its own budget, chartfield strings, URI Foundation accounts, student scholarships, and research funds.
Central Data for Fall 2019 show that GWS delivers many credit hours, 2,010 per 6.8 FTE for a 297.8 ratio.
When compared to the overall URI's Central Data from F2018, GWS has been delivering a lot of value on minimal resources for many years now. 2.

Describe how current institutional resources will be deployed or extra institutional resources will be obtained to support the organizational change (e.g., describe unit elimination, staff reallocations and/or external sources of monies) GWS will administer its budget as it has done previous years to support a half-time administrative assistance, faculty salaries, 2-3 student workers, and general operational costs.
No extra resources are required for the organizational change.
Justifications for current resources: Personnel Costs: • Administrative Assistant, half-time: staff person required to execute daily administrative duties like ordering supplies and accounts payable, faculty research and travel accounts, budgetary duties as well as support the chair, faculty, and students' with academic procedures.
Administrative staff also provides programming and social event support.
GWS runs from 3-4 events every semester that include the Dana Shugar, Carlson, and other colloquia.

A Half-time staff person is currently sufficient for the operation of GWS. • Chair: Teaching Professor of Sociology and Anthropology o Primary department Sociology and Anthropology o Teaching duties 50% GWS and 50% Sociology o Chair allowance of $5000 and 11% summer stipend • Faculty: o 1 full-time Full Professor III, 1.0 FTE o 1 full-time Clinical Associate Professor, 1.0 FTE o 1 two-thirds Assistant Professor, 0.75 FTE o 1 one-third Associate Professor, 0.25 FTE

9 o 4 limited and unlimited joint-appointments--no GWS budgetary impact o 17-20 PTFs (represent 27% of all teaching resources) Operating Expenses: Expect to stay in the same range as current budgetary allocation. Capital Expenses: No new capital expenses required. o Current office space allocations adequate: Roosevelt 317, 315, 313, 311, 314, 316 o Computers, copy machine, printers, and other technology: all updated and functional. o Furniture: no new furniture expenses anticipated for current staff and offices Future Growth Projections: GWS expects to grow majors from an average of 40 to 65 and minors from 40 to 60 over the next three years. The establishment of the Queer Studies minor (to be initiated in Fall 21) and other curricular innovations in the areas of black feminisms and masculinities studies will increase student interest in GWS. GWS also will recruit students in these areas and continue to encourage double majors. GWS recently revised its Graduate Certificate Program, and through consistent outreach efforts aims to increase graduate students from an average of 3-5 to 7-10 annually. GWS anticipates that by AY 2022, GWS will need to reassess its teaching and operational needs and better align resources with this growth.

Article III, Section 7 – Ethical conduct. The people of the State of Rhode Island believe that public officials and employees must adhere to the highest standards of ethical conduct, respect the public trust and the rights of all persons, be open, accountable and responsive, avoid the appearance of impropriety and not use their position for private gain or advantage.
WHAT IS “ETHICAL” CONDUCT?

Ethics: a standard or philosophy of right and wrong human behavior based on logical reasoning So… “Ethical Conduct” is the type of behavior that a logical person would agree is the “right” thing to do under the circumstances But - People have different ideas about what makes behavior “right” or “wrong”
Ethics based on CULTURE – Many people think that whether something is “ethical” depends on the setting in which it occurs, taking into account the local culture, habits and customs.

Ethics based on CONSEQUENCES - Ethical or unethical conduct is determined by examining the results. Ethical conduct is behavior that results in more positive results than negative results, in quantity and quality.

Ethics based on CHARACTER - Ethical conduct is determined by asking, “What would a virtuous person do under the circumstances?” The focus is on one’s character and motives. I am an honest, upstanding person, so how could I violate the Code of Ethics?

Focus on your ACTION, not the result ! ! ! The Code of Ethics tells us what actions to avoid, without regard to culture, consequence, or character. Ethical or unethical conduct is determined NOT by looking at the results, but at the conduct itself and judging its inherent rightness or wrongness.
Who is subject to the Code of Ethics? All elected and appointed officials and employees of state and local government, boards, commissions and agencies shall be subject to the Code of Ethics.

(9) Members – appointed by the Governor ► Advisory Powers ► Investigative Powers ► Adjudicative Powers ► Removal Powers While serving on the Ethics Commission, members are prohibited from holding or campaigning for public office, holding office in any political party or political committee, and participating in or contributing to any political campaign.

• Executive Director/Chief Prosecutor • Investigators (3) • Senior Staff Attorney • Office Manager • Education Coordinator/Staff Attorney • Financial Disclosure Officer • Staff Attorneys (2) • Ancillary Staff (2) The services of Legal Counsel are retained independent of the Executive Director or other Commission employees. A person subject to the Code of Ethics . . . may not participate in any matter in which he or she has an interest, financial or otherwise, which is in substantial conflict with the proper discharge of his or her duties in the public interest. A substantial conflict of interest occurs if it is reasonably foreseeable that he or she or any family member or business associate, or any business by which he or she is employed or represents, will derive a direct monetary gain or suffer a direct monetary loss by reason of his or her official activity.

Reasonably foreseeable The conflict need not be certain to occur, but the probability must be greater than “conceivably.” Business Associates Your “business associates” are any persons or entities that you are joined with to achieve a common financial objective. These include not only your business partners, but also people you have hired such as an attorney, accountant, realtor, contractor, etc. These also include any businesses or organizations, even if not-for-profit, for which you are an officer or serve on the Board of Directors.
Ongoing Business Association parties conducting ongoing business transactions outstanding accounts anticipated future relationship
Who are my family members? Whether by blood, marriage, or adoption: Spouse Grandchildren Parents Aunts/Uncles Children Nieces/Nephews Siblings First Cousins Grandparents

A conflict of interest is a situation where a person’s public duties impact, or involve, his or her private life. ► It is not unethical to have a conflict of interest. ► It does not violate the Code of Ethics to have a conflict of interest. ► It is not the conflict that is the problem; rather, the potential problem is in a failure to identify and manage the conflict.

Do I have a conflict of interest? Ask yourself . . . Is it “reasonably foreseeable” that: A decision I am helping to make as part of my public duties, will result in a financial benefit or detriment to: Me; or My family or household member; or My outside employer; or My business associate?

Ask yourself: Even if there is no financial impact, is a family member, household member, employer or business associate a party to, or participating in, the matter being discussed? If the answer is “Yes,” then you have a conflict of interest and you must recuse from any participation in the matter.

HOW TO RECUSE 1. Complete a Statement of Conflict of Interest form. 2. Present the original to your presiding officer, appointing authority, director, or immediate supervisor. 3. Send a copy to the Ethics Commission.

Nepotism - You may not participate in any matter as part of your public duties if there is reason to believe or expect that any person within your family or a household member . . . • is a party to or participant in such matter; or • will derive a direct monetary gain; or • will suffer a direct monetary loss; or • obtain an employment advantage.

These prohibitions apply regardless of whether a family or household member is objectively the most qualified candidate for a job, or is deserving of promotion. The policy underlying the prohibitions against nepotism in the Code recognizes that it is difficult for any person to be truly objective when considering matters impacting family/household members and, additionally, furthers the constitutionally founded goal of avoiding the appearance of impropriety.

Scenario – Andy is a member of the Anytown Town Council. The Town has just released a Request for Proposals (RFP) for the construction of a municipal playground. Billy is Andy’s nephew. Billy’s construction company submits a bid in response to the RFP.

Advocacy/Supervision – You may not participate in the supervision, evaluation, appointment, classification, promotion, transfer, or discipline of any person in your family or a household member.

Advocacy/Supervision – You may not delegate to a subordinate any tasks relating to the supervision, evaluation, appointment, classification, promotion, transfer, or discipline of any person in your family or household member.

Budgets– You may not participate in discussions or decision-making regarding a budgetary line item that would address or affect the employment, compensation, or benefits of any person in your family or a household member.

Budgets– You may participate in discussion and decision-making relative to approving or rejecting an entire budget as a whole - provided . . . the person within your family or household member is impacted by the entire budget as a member of a significant and definable class of persons, and not individually or to any greater extent than any other similarly situated member of the class.

Collective Bargaining/Employment Contracts– You may not participate in negotiations relative to an employee contract or collective bargaining which addresses or affects the employment, compensation, or benefits of any person in your family or a household member.

Collective Bargaining/Employment Contracts– You may participate in a decision to accept or reject an entire employee contract or collective bargaining agreement as a whole - provided . . . the person within your family or household member is impacted by the entire contract or agreement as a member of a significant and definable class of persons, and not individually or to any greater extent than any other similarly situated member of the class.

► Recusal is not the same as abstaining, which may mean that the public official will not vote, but has participated in discussions on a matter. ► Recusal means that you are not participating in deliberations or debates, making recommendations, giving advice, considering findings, or in any other way assuming responsibility for or participating in any aspect of the work or decision-making relating to the matter where there are potential conflicts of interest.

Recusal does not mean that the public official must leave the room if it is an open meeting, although it is best practice to do so. However, if the public body is in executive session, once the official has recused, he or she has no more right to be in the room than any other member of the general public.

No person subject to the Code of Ethics may enter into any contract with a state or municipal agency unless . . . the contract has been awarded through an open and public process, including prior public notice and subsequent public disclosure of all proposals considered and contracts awarded.

Contracts for professional services which have been customarily awarded without competitive bidding shall not be subject to competitive bidding if awarded through a process of public notice and disclosure of financial details.

STATE VENDORS PROVIDING GOODS OR SERVICES TO PUBLIC OFFICIALS

No state vendor shall provide goods or services for less than fair market value for the personal use of a procurement official of a state agency – if – the vendor has sold goods and services during the preceding twenty-four (24) months to the state agency – or – if the vendor knows or has reason to know he or she will be submitting a bid or making a proposal for the sale of goods or services within the succeeding twenty-four (24) months to the state agency.

No procurement official of a state agency shall accept goods or services for his or her personal use for less than the fair market value from a state vendor who has sold goods or services to the agency during the preceding twenty-four (24) months – or – who the procurement official knows or has reason to know will be submitting a bid or making a proposal for the sale of goods or services to the agency within the succeeding twenty-four (24) months.

Secondary Employment You may have a private or public sector job in addition to your state/municipal position; however, you may not accept outside employment that impairs your independence of judgment or that induces you to disclose confidential government information.

When considering potential conflicts of interest regarding secondary employment, the Commission examines a number of factors: • nexus between public duties & private employment • whether such work is completed outside normal work hours & without use of public resources • whether the official/employee would appear before own agency • whether such work would be conducted outside of areas over which official/employee has decision-making jurisdiction • whether official/employee would use his or her public position to solicit business or customers

The Appearance of Impropriety The appearance of impropriety is a phrase referring to a situation which to a layperson without knowledge of the specific circumstances might seem to raise ethics questions.

The Appearance of Impropriety When enacting the Code of Ethics, the General Assembly included as one of its legislative purposes the elimination of impropriety. The legislature did not, however, make the appearance of impropriety a violation of the law.
